Question 1: Is OpenDT accurate enough for what-if analysis on SURF?

Change: Calibration Off (the calibrator would fit r to the ground truth again after each change of hosts).

Yes, its MAPE stays under 10%No, its MAPE goes over 10%

Hint: 10% is the community-accepted error rate; see the Real-time MAPE.

Solution: Yes: MAPE about 6%. OpenDT under-estimates the ground truth in almost every minute of the day, more in the first 6 hours (MAPE 10.4%) than after (MAPE 4.6%); the OpenDT paper identifies the same underestimation trend.

Question 4: How far is the power draw with 2,770 hosts from the guess, and why?

About 10x, as each host runs jobsAbout 4x, as the extra hosts are idleAbout the same

Hint: Look at the idle hosts and at the power they draw.

Solution: About 4x (84 vs. 22 kW): the jobs are the same, so the 2,493 extra hosts are idle, and an idle host still draws 25 W (2,493 x 25 W = 62 kW). Over-provisioning could lead to sustainability concerns, both environmental and financial, where energy (and thus, money) is wasted by idle infrastructure.

Question 5: With 138 and 69 hosts, how much power does SURF save, and what happens to the jobs?

Change: Hosts 138, then Apply; later, Hosts 69.

Much power, and the jobs run as beforeLittle power with 138 hosts, and some jobs wait

Hint: An idle host draws 25 W; look at the jobs waiting.

Solution: With 138 hosts, only 16% less power (switching off 139 idle hosts saves 139 x 25 W, about 3.5 kW), and some jobs wait: at peak, more than 138 jobs need a host. With 69 hosts, jobs wait more than a day on average, and hundreds still wait at the end of the day; the power is lower because these jobs have not run yet. Under-provisioning ICT infrastructure could lead to performance concerns, system faults, and, ultimately, system failures.

HintSolution
BackNext

Question 6: Which costs of switching hosts off and on again does this estimate leave out?

Hint: What does a host do before it can run a job, and who decides to switch it off?

Solution: Boot time: hosts need minutes to boot, so new jobs wait when no spare host is free. A human-in-the-loop, aiming to ensure the correct and ethical operation of the process, oversees at least the major decisions (e.g., switching off hosts) and can intervene at any time.

HintSolution

Question 9: Does the best r stay the same, and what does this mean for a twin that runs for weeks?

It stays the sameIt changes over time

Hint: Hardware behavior varies with temperature, aging, and firmware updates.

Solution: No; the best r changes between 5 and 9 from day to day. Static simulation models can drift and introduce errors as the time horizon increases: hardware behavior varies with temperature, aging, and firmware updates, while workload characteristics evolve over time. Therefore, OpenDT recalibrates continuously.

HintSolution

Question 12: Should SURF migrate its workload to RO, and what else does the human-in-the-loop weigh?

Hint: Think beyond the carbon intensity of the grid.

Solution: The saving is small (6% vs. NL), and NL is greener than RO in a third of the hours. Before migrating, the human-in-the-loop considers, e.g., (1) the energy and time to move data and jobs over the network, (2) the latency for the users, (3) the rules on where data may be stored, (4) the free capacity and the cost of the remote datacenter, and (5) the CO2 emitted to build new hardware.

HintSolution
Back
